newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin calm on Belarus, pulls out Chechnya troops.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin calm on Belarus, pulls out Chechnya troops.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin, dealing with a number of frontier issues on his first full day out of hospital, made a major concession to Chechen rebels to seal a peace accord on Saturday and played down a setback for Moscow in Belarus.
He ordered the withdrawal of the last Russian troops in Chechnya in what his spokesman said was a "goodwill gesture", but which the separatists made a condition for lasting peace.
The move, which returns the military deployment to what it was before Yeltsin ordered the army to crush the secessionists in December 1994, smacked of an acceptance of defeat.

It was immediately followed by the signing of a framework document between Chechen government leader Aslan Maskhadov and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, which aims to define relations between Moscow and the breakaway region.

Progress toward peace in Chechnya was overshadowed, however, by the collapse of a Russian-brokered compromise in neighbouring Belarus. Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko seemed set once more on a collision course with his opponents in parliament over a referendum on Sunday on increasing Lukashenko's powers.
Moscow's initial reaction, however, was a mask of calm.

A spokesman for Yeltsin, who had called Friday's compromise a "great victory" for Russian diplomacy, said the first major step to ending the tension had been taken and that it was a matter of time before the crisis was fully resolved.

Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing: "Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) considers there is no need to jump to conclusions. He very much counts on the process of fulfilling the agreement being continued and brought to a conclusion."

Yeltsin had received the latest reports on Saturday morning at the Barvikha sanatorium near Moscow where he is convalescing from heart surgery, the spokesman said. The president felt it was natural there should have been opposition to Friday's deal.

"You should understand the president's statement as saying there is a sharp drop in tension, that the worst of the crisis is over," Yastrzhembsky said. "But that does not mean that the crisis itself has already been happily settled."

Moscow, which agreed to a two-state union with its closest ally among the former Soviet states in April, approves of Lukashenko's pursuit of closer ties but worries that the lack of economic reform in Belarus could be a burden to Russia.
The Kremlin would be particularly worried if events in its western neighbour were to turn violent. But analysts do not think Moscow is prepared to intervene militarily.
With Yeltsin confined to Barvikha and Chernomyrdin dealing with the Chechens, Moscow's immediate diplomatic response was muted and seemed limited to searching for hopeful signs.
"I do not think all is lost," said Gennady Seleznyov, the communist speaker of the State Duma lower house, who took part in Chernomyrdin's negotiations in Minsk.
"Like it or not, Russia is a guarantor. This agreement does not infringe rights of either party," he told ORT television.

In his first meeting with a foreign leader since his heart bypass surgery on November 5, Yeltsin discussed with Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev the touchy issue of ethnic Russians living beyond Russia's old Soviet internal border.
Yastrzhembsky said that, in 20 minutes of talks, Yeltsin asked Nazarbayev to safeguard the rights of Russian speakers.

In another sign of Yeltsin's rapid return to health, his spokesman said the president expected to host a summit of leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States in Moscow early in January. He discussed this with Nazarbayev.
